question: In chronic osteomyelitis, the 'involucrum' refers to which of the following?

answers.text: The dead, avascular fragment of cortical bone surrounded by pus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes the sequestrum — the dead bone nidus that antibiotics cannot penetrate because it lacks blood supply.

answers.text: A new sheath of reactive bone formed by the elevated periosteum around the sequestrum

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The involucrum is the living shell of new periosteal bone that surrounds the sequestrum. It has cloacae (openings) through which pus tracks to form sinus tracts.

answers.text: A sinus tract connecting the infected bone to the skin surface

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A sinus tract is the opening through which pus discharges — it is formed through cloacae in the involucrum, not the involucrum itself.

answers.text: Granulation tissue filling the medullary cavity in chronic infection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Granulation tissue fills the cavity but does not constitute the involucrum. The involucrum is specifically the reactive cortical bone shell.

overallFeedback.feedback: Revisit block 6. Sequestrum = dead avascular bone fragment (the nidus); involucrum = new periosteal bone sheath surrounding it. Confusing these two leads to errors in both diagnosis and operative planning.

Well done. Remember the pair: sequestrum (dead bone inside) + involucrum (living bone shell outside). Surgical removal of the sequestrum (sequestrectomy) is mandatory because antibiotics cannot reach avascular dead bone.
